items.title: Spy Shots Catch Mercedes Prototype Driving Around with No Body Like a Production Death Kart
items.summary:
For years, we’ve been told that EVs would fundamentally change the way we think about automotive body engineering, giving us access to a true “skateboard” chassis that could underpin virtually anything from a sports car to a semi truck. It appears that Mercedes has come up with the best possible application of this technology in the current EV era : this kick-ass, all-electric death kart… thing. 

Certainly this open chassis is serving as a testbed for something more substantial than what we can see here, but if you ask us, we’ll take it just the way it is—light, open, and regardless of what those motors may be intended to power, likely very quick relative to whatever finished product it will eventually become. 

Neither we nor our spies have any idea exactly what these engineers are testing, but if it is indeed an early chassis mule, it’s likely for some sort of sports car. The layout allows for two passengers and not much more, and we can see the components of an air suspension fitted here, along with what appear to be aluminum upper and lower wishbones in the front suspension (along with a traditional anti-roll bar). 

Stefan Baldauf / SB-Medien 

While the mule’s proportions suggest a sports car, we shouldn’t jump to conclusions in that regard. It looks long and low, certainly, but it’s fitted with some awfully tall, skinny wheels and tires for a performance car. The rears appear to be some hard-worn Continentals with the branding scuffed off. 

Inside, there’s a full steering wheel (not necessarily a given these days) and some sport seats bolted to a wooden floor pan…
items.t: Be Brave: Mercedes Caught Testing a Death Kart That They Should Absolutely Sell

items.title: The Kia Telluride’s Only Fault Is Its Awful Climate Controls
items.summary:
The Kia Telluride is one of those vehicles that makes you wonder why people spend so much more money for the same basic product. It’s an extremely well-rounded big SUV that beats the competition soundly on value. But it’s not perfect. Both my colleague Joel Feder and I drove one in recent weeks, and came to the same conclusion: Kia’s climate-control touchscreen has got to go.

If you haven’t paid much attention to Kia design in recent years, the brand decided to stuff a tiny touch-sensitive display between the instrument cluster and central infotainment screen on its latest slate of models. This panel exclusively controls heating and air conditioning, which, on the surface, sounds great—here at  The Drive , we’re fans of more tiny screens with individual functions rather than bigger ones.

The problem is placement. Because of where this little display lives, it’s completely obscured by the right side of the steering wheel from a normal driving perspective. At least, it was for Joel and me. It’s no wonder this design choice annoyed us, because we’re both 5 feet, 10 inches tall.

Adam Ismail 

This quirk isn’t exclusive to the Telluride; the Kia K4 has it, as do the Seltos and EV3. I will admit, the first time I saw it on the K4, I thought it looked cool, but my fondness for it diminished with continued exposure in other vehicles. It’s one of those ideas that sounds good on paper and appears nice in a photo, until you encounter it in a practical setting. That’s when it becomes clear why automakers rarely put anything in that spot on the dash.

items.title: This Jeep Wrangler With a Lamborghini Body Kit Is Like a Real-Life Hot Wheels Car
items.summary:
There’s nothing cooler than low-dollar, high-creativity car projects. And this lifted Jeep YJ, wearing a Lamborghini body kit made for a Pontiac Fiero , is one of the most creative things I’ve seen in a while! It’s the brainchild of Kyle Lewis, a gearhead in North Carolina who had an old Wrangler, stumbled on a neglected knockoff Countach, and turned them into this delightfully twisted caricature on wheels.

Lewis has posted quite a bit about the “Jeepborghini” on his Instagram page (the vehicle has its own IG and YouTube channel , too). “I was inspired to build this because I saw a Lamborghini body kit on a Pontiac Fiero parked at a parking lot for over 30 years. And I said, ‘I want it.’ So I bought it and started from there,” Lewis said.

What’s left of the Jeep is sitting on 35-inch tires. Since the vehicle’s so small, they look like they came off a monster truck. But perhaps the most impressive thing to me is that the scissor doors seem to be functioning properly. I’d imagine the fitment would be wobbly after decades of rotting in the sun, but I guess the kit car was made of tougher stuff than I’d have expected!

Lewis has some kind of speaker setup in the back, where a real Countach’s engine would be, completeing the video-game-character-car vibe quite nicely.

items.title: How Tremec Figured Out a Manual Transmission for the C8 Corvette When GM Wouldn’t Do It
items.summary:
When Tremec told the world last year that it had developed a manual gearbox for the automatic-only C8 Chevrolet Corvette, the announcement created quite a stir. That buzz wasn’t limited to enthusiast chatter on social media; even Corvette Executive Chief Engineer Tony Roma commented on the existence (or lack thereof, at the time) of Tremec’s gearbox . Things got a bit tense, perhaps, and some were left with the impression that Tremec was dunking on GM for lacking the imagination necessary to make a manual C8 happen.

The real story, of course, is quite different. I touched on this in my brief drive of the first manual-swapped C8 by Peitz Performance , but here’s the longer version: GM’s decision had nothing to do with its engineering capabilities and everything to do with budgets. Roma has made no bones about it: a key component of the Corvette formula is affordability, and simply offering a second gearbox meant doubling the budget for an already whole-cloth transmission redesign.

“Transmissions are super expensive,” Roma told us on The Drivecast ( the full transcript is published here on the site ). “When we had C5, C6, and C7, we could use basically the same manual transmission architecture that had been around and slowly developed over like 30 years, and it was mostly paid for, and we were doing slight upgrades on it, and it cost reasonable amounts of money to keep it in production.”

items.title: Toyota Explains How It’s Trying to Fix Its Big Tundra Problem
items.summary:
Toyota, the world’s largest automaker, knows it has a problem: its Tundra truck engine is threatening its rock-solid reputation for reliability .

Now, the updated 2027 Toyota Tundra is arriving at dealerships and aims to address many issues with the current truck including but not limited to safety concerns with towing, infotainment limitations, ride quality issues, and more. Of course, Toyota’s angling for its change in machining processes for engine production to also hopefully fix its reliability issues. On the latest episode of The Drivecast , Toyota Tundra and Sequoia Assistant Chief Engineer Rob Crawford sat down exclusively with The Drive   to sort through the changes.

The Tundra ended up at the center of Toyota’s engine failure crisis . If you read The Drive or listen to this podcast, you know what I’m talking about. But for those who don’t, Toyota took a big swing when it introduced a 3.4 liter twin turbo V6 known as the V35A FTS in the current generation Tundra pickup and Sequoia SUV in 2022. It replaced the hardy 5.7 liter V8 used by those models for over a decade.

And at the time, a lot of people wondered if swapping a simple proven engine for a new high stress one would lead to problems. Sure enough, it did. The new V6 started destroying itself at notably high rates. As we’ve reported at length, including on this podcast back in June, the issue surrounds tiny bits of metal debris called swarf that get left behind in the engine block during manufacturing. Those shavings then adhere to the main bearing and cause knocking, rough idle, or total engine failure.…

The good news is that this law will ban foolishness like BMW’s now-infamous subscription seat-warmers , which the company backtracked on pretty much immediately after widespread internet backlash . The bad news is that the entire “features as a service” fad will be left largely intact, because virtually all subscription services offered in modern cars require that they phone home to some sort of server in order to function. That includes features like connected navigation, emergency roadside assistance, and in-car hotspot plans. Here’s the actual language (emphasis added by the author):
